source_text: Καὶ ἐκεῖνος μὲν γὰρ τοσούτοις τρέφεται σιτίοις, ὅσα οὐκ ἂν ἀπαιτήσειε τὸν μοναχὸν ὕπνον βαθύν· τὸν δὲ ἡ τρυφὴ κατακοιμίζει καὶ ὁ πότος μέχρις ἡμέρας αὐτῆς ἐν τῇ κλίνῃ κατέχων. Ἔστι τοίνυν τῷ μὲν μοναχῷ καὶ ἀμπεχόνη καὶ τράπεζα μετρία, καὶ σύσσιτοι τῆς αὐτῆς ἀρετῆς ἀθληταί· τὸν βασιλέα δὲ λίθοις τε ἀνάγκη καὶ χρυσῷ καλλωπίζεσθαι, τράπεζάν τε παρατίθεσθαι λαμπρὰν, καὶ χρῆσθαι συσσίτοις, εἰ μὲν ἄφρων εἴη, τῆς ἑαυτοῦ κακίας ἀξίοις, εἰ δὲ νοῦν ἔχοι καὶ σωφρονοίη, χρηστοῖς ἴσως καὶ δικαίοις, πολὺ δὲ λειπομένοις τῆς ἐκείνων ἀρετῆς. Οὕτω κἂν φιλοσοφῇ βασιλεὺς, οὐδὲ κατὰ μικρὸν ἐγγὺς ἐλθεῖν τῆς τοῦ μονάζοντος καλοκαγαθίας δυνήσεται. Καὶ γὰρ ἐν ὁδοιπορίαις βαρύς ἐστι τοῖς ὑπηκόοις, καὶ πόλιν οἰκῶν, καὶ εἰρήνης ἀπολαύων, καὶ πολέμων ἁπτόμενος, φόρους τε εἰσπραττόμενος, καὶ στρατεύματα συγκροτῶν, καὶ αἰχμαλώτους ἄγων, καὶ νικῶν, καὶ ἡττώμενος· ἡττώμενος μὲν γὰρ τῶν οἰκείων κακῶν ἀναπίμπλησι τοὺς ἀρχομένους, νικῶν δὲ ἀφόρητος γίνεται, καλλωπιζόμενός τε τοῖς τροπαίοις, καὶ μέγα φρονῶν, καὶ τοῖς στρατιώταις παρέχων ἄδειαν ἁρπάζειν, συλᾷν, τοὺς ὁδοιπόρους ἀδικεῖν, τὰς πόλεις ἐν τῇ καθέδρᾳ πολιορκεῖν, τὰς τῶν πενήτων πορθεῖν οἰκίας, τοὺς ὑποδεξαμένους εἰσπράττεσθαι καθ' ἑκάστην ἡμέραν ἃ μηδεὶς ἐπιτρέπει νόμος, ἐπὶ προφάσει τινὸς ἔθους ἀρχαίου παρανόμου τε καὶ ἀδίκου. Καὶ τὸν μὲν πλούσιον ἔβλαψεν οὐδὲν ὁ βασιλεὺς τοῖς τοιούτοις κακοῖς, τὴν πενίαν δὲ ἐκάκωσεν, ὥσπερ ὡς ἀληθῶς αἰσχυνόμενος τοὺς εὐπόρους. Οὐ μὴν ὅ γε μοναχὸς οὕτως, ἀλλ' ἅμα τε ὤφθη, καὶ πλουσίων καὶ πενήτων χάριν τινὰ κομίζων ἦλθε καὶ τούτοις κἀκείνοις ὁμοίως, ἱματίῳ μὲν ἑνὶ δι' ἔτους χρώμενος, ὕδωρ δὲ πίνων ἥδιον, ἢ θαυμαστὸν οἶνον ἕτεροι· ὑπὲρ ἑαυτοῦ μὲν οὐδεμίαν, οὔτε μικρὰν, οὔτε μείζω χάριν παρὰ τῶν πλουσίων αἰτῶν, ὑπὲρ δὲ τῶν ἐν ἐνδείᾳ πολλάς τε καὶ συνεχεῖς, ἀμφοτέροις λυσιτελούσας, τοῖς τε παρέχουσι, καὶ τοῖς κομίζεσθαι μέλλουσιν. Οὕτω κοινός ἐστιν ἰατρὸς καὶ πλουσίων καὶ πενήτων ὁμοίως, τοὺς μὲν ἁμαρτημάτων ἐλευθερῶν διὰ τῆς ἀγαθῆς νουθεσίας, τοῖς δὲ λύων τὴν ἔνδειαν. Βασιλεὺς δὲ τάς τε εἰσφορὰς κουφοτέρας εἶναι κελεύων, τοὺς πλουσίους μᾶλλον, ἢ τὴν πενίαν ὠφέλησε· καὶ τὰ ἐναντία ποιῶν, τοὺς μικρὰ κεκτημένους ἔβλαψε. Τὸν μὲν γὰρ πλούσιον ὀλίγα ἂν βλάψειεν ἡ χαλεπότης τῶν εἰσφορῶν, τὰς δὲ τῶν πενήτων οἰκίας ὥσπερ χειμάῤῥους παρασύρει, οἰμωγῆς πιμπλῶσα τὰς κώμας, καὶ οὔτε γῆρας ἐλεεινὸν τοῖς εἰσπραττομένοις τοὺς φόρους, οὔτε χηρεία γυναικῶν, οὐκ ὀρφανία παίδων, ἀλλὰ κωμάζουσι πάντα τὸν χρόνον, κοινοί τινες πολέμιοι τῆς χώρας, ἅπερ οὐκ ἐξήνεγκεν ἡ γῆ, ταῦτα τοὺς γεωργοὺς εἰσπραττόμενοι. δʹ. Φέρε δὴ κἀκεῖνο ἐξετάσωμεν, τί μὲν ὁ μοναχὸς, τί δὲ ὁ βασιλεὺς τοῖς ὑπηκόοις χαρίζεται. Οὐκοῦν ὁ μὲν χρυσὸν, ὁ δὲ πνεύματος χάριν· καὶ ὁ μὲν ἔλυσε πενίαν, ὅταν ᾖ χρηστὸς, ὁ δὲ ψυχὰς τυραννουμένας ὑπὸ δαιμόνων ἠλευθέρωσε ταῖς προσευχαῖς. Κἂν συμβῇ τινα τοιαύταις χειμάζεσθαι συμφοραῖς, τὸν βασιλέα μὲν ὥσπερ τὰ ἄψυχα παρέρχεται, ἐπὶ δὲ τὴν τῶν μοναχῶν οἰκίαν καταφεύγει, ὥσπερ ὁ λύκον ὑποφεύγων, καταφεύγων δὲ ἐπ' ἄνδρα θηρευτὴν ξίφος ἐν τῇ χειρὶ φέροντα· ὅπερ γὰρ τῷ θηρευτῇ ξίφος, τοῦτο προσευχὴ τῷ μονάζοντι.
thought_title: The monk's common benefit versus the king's burdens
orientation: Chrysostom continues contrasting the daily life and social effect of the monk with that of the king, showing the monk as a common physician to rich and poor while the king's exactions crush the poor.
pass_a_gloss: For that one is fed with so many foods, as many as would not demand deep sleep from the monk; but luxury puts him to sleep and drink, holding him in the bed until day itself. So then for the monk there is both modest clothing and a modest table, and fellow-diners who are athletes of the same virtue; but the king is compelled to be adorned with stones and gold, and to have a splendid table set before him, and to use fellow-diners who, if he should be foolish, are worthy of his own wickedness, but if he should have sense and be self-controlled, are perhaps good and just, but far inferior to the virtue of those men. Thus even if a king should live the way of life, he will not be able to come near, not even by a little, to the excellence of the one who lives alone. For both in journeys he is heavy to his subjects, and dwelling in a city, and enjoying peace, and taking hold of wars, and collecting tributes, and assembling armies, and leading captives, and conquering, and being defeated; for when defeated he fills the ruled with his own evils, but when conquering he becomes unbearable, adorning himself with trophies, and thinking great things, and giving to the soldiers license to seize, to plunder, to wrong the travelers, to besiege the cities in their seat, to ravage the houses of the poor, to exact from those who received them each day what no law permits, on the pretext of some ancient custom lawless and unjust. And the rich man the king harmed not at all with such evils, but he afflicted poverty, as if truly being ashamed before the wealthy. Not so, however, the monk, but at once he appeared, and came bringing some favor to rich and poor, and to these and those alike, using one garment through the year, and drinking water more sweetly than others drink marvelous wine; asking for himself no favor, neither small nor greater, from the rich, but for those in need many and continuous favors, profitable to both, to those who provide and to those who are about to receive. Thus he is a common physician of rich and poor alike, freeing the former from sins through good admonition, and for the latter loosening their need. But the king, both ordering the taxes to be lighter, benefited the rich rather than poverty; and doing the opposite, harmed those who possess little. For the rich man the harshness of the taxes would harm little, but the houses of the poor it sweeps away like a torrent, filling the villages with wailing, and neither pitiable old age of those from whom the tributes are exacted, nor widowhood of women, nor orphanhood of children, but they revel all the time, common enemies of the land, exacting from the farmers those things which the earth did not produce. 4. Come then, let us examine also that: what the monk grants to his subjects, and what the king. Therefore the one grants gold, but the other grace of spirit; and the one loosened poverty, whenever he is good, but the other freed souls tyrannized by demons through prayers. And if it should happen that someone is storm-tossed by such misfortunes, he passes by the king as if lifeless things, but flees to the house of the monks, just as one fleeing a wolf, fleeing to a hunter man bearing a sword in his hand; for what the sword is to the hunter, this prayer is to the one who lives alone.

choices.why: The term denotes the classical ideal of noble goodness; rendering as 'excellence' preserves the moral quality without importing a specifically Christian term.
The participle expresses the king's shrinking from or shame before the rich, explaining why he spares them and harms the poor.
The clause refers to the king, not the monk; the contrast is between the king's gold and the monk's spiritual grace, with the king's benefit to poverty conditional on his being good.
rejected: when he is good, loosens poverty (referring to monk)

choices.why: The phrase describes the king as inanimate or unresponsive to the sufferer's need, emphasizing the monk as the true refuge.
The phrase likely refers to the soldiers' occupation or encampment; rendering literally preserves the spatial image of besieging cities from their position.
The phrase marks the tax collectors as public enemies; 'common' preserves the sense of shared or universal hostility.

pass_b_english: For the monk is fed only with so much food as would not demand deep sleep, unlike the king, while luxury and drink lull him to sleep, keeping him in bed until day itself. The monk, then, has modest clothing and a modest table, and fellow-diners who are athletes of the same excellence. The king, by necessity, is adorned with stones and gold, has a splendid table set before him, and uses fellow-diners who, if he is foolish, are worthy of his own wickedness, but if he has sense and is self-controlled, are perhaps good and just, yet fall far short of the monk's excellence. Thus even if a king pursues the way of life, he will not be able to come even a little near the excellence of the monk. For on journeys he is a burden to his subjects, whether he dwells in a city, enjoys peace, or takes up wars, collecting taxes, assembling armies, leading captives, conquering, and being defeated. When he is defeated, he fills his subjects with his own evils; when he conquers, he becomes unbearable, adorning himself with trophies, thinking great thoughts, and giving soldiers license to seize, to plunder, to wrong travelers, to occupy and besiege cities, to ravage the houses of the poor, and to exact from those who quartered them each day what no law permits, under the pretext of some ancient custom that is lawless and unjust. The king does no harm to the rich with such evils, but he afflicts the poor, as if truly being ashamed before the wealthy. The monk, however, is not like this. As soon as he appears, he comes bringing some grace to rich and poor alike, to these and to those equally, using one garment through the year, drinking water more sweetly than others drink marvelous wine. For himself he asks no favor from the rich, neither small nor great, but for those in need he asks many and continuous favors, beneficial to both those who give and those who are about to receive. Thus he is a common physician of rich and poor alike, freeing the former from sins through good counsel, and relieving the latter's want. But the king, when he orders the taxes to be lighter, benefits the rich more than the poor; and when he does the opposite, he harms those who possess little. For the harshness of taxes would harm the rich only a little, but it sweeps away the houses of the poor like a torrent, filling the villages with lamentation. Neither pitiable old age, nor the widowhood of women, nor the orphanhood of children stops those who collect the taxes; they revel all the time, common enemies of the land, exacting from the farmers what the earth has not produced.

Come then, let us also examine this: what does the monk grant to his subjects, and what does the king? The king grants gold, the monk the grace of the Spirit. The one loosens poverty whenever he is good; the other has freed souls tyrannized by demons through prayers. And if someone happens to be storm-tossed by such misfortunes, the king is passed by like the inanimate, and he flees to the house of the monks, like one fleeing from a wolf and taking refuge with a hunter who carries a sword in his hand. For what the sword is to the hunter, prayer is to the monk.

problems.quote: he comes bringing some grace to rich and poor alike, to these and to those equally
problems.source_quote: πλουσίων καὶ πενήτων χάριν τινὰ κομίζων ἦλθε καὶ τούτοις κἀκείνοις ὁμοίως
problems.why: χάριν τινὰ is 'some grace/favor', but the point is the monk brings grace to both; however, 'to these and to those equally' is redundant and slightly changes emphasis—the Greek emphasizes he comes to both alike.
problems.fix: he comes bringing some grace alike to rich and poor, to these and to those equally

problems.why: τὴν πενίαν is 'the poor' (abstract for concrete), not the abstraction 'poverty'. Greek often uses abstract nouns for classes of people.
problems.ruling: τὴν πενίαν here = 'the poor' (concrete), not abstraction 'poverty'; 'afflicts poverty' misleads readers.

problems.quote: benefits the rich more than poverty
problems.source_quote: τοὺς πλουσίους μᾶλλον, ἢ τὴν πενίαν ὠφέλησε
problems.why: Again τὴν πενίαν = 'the poor', not 'poverty'. The king helps the rich more than he helps the poor.
problems.fix: benefits the rich more than the poor
problems.ruling: τὴν πενίαν = 'the poor' (concrete), not 'poverty'; 'benefits the rich more than poverty' misleads.

edits.old: he comes bringing some grace to rich and poor alike, to these and to those equally
edits.new: he comes bringing some grace alike to rich and poor, to these and to those equally

edits.old: benefits the rich more than poverty
edits.new: benefits the rich more than the poor

fixed: χάριν τινά is 'some grace/favor'; the Greek emphasizes he comes to both alike, so 'alike' should modify 'rich and poor' rather than being separated.
τὴν πενίαν is abstract for concrete, meaning 'the poor', not the abstraction 'poverty'.
τὴν πενίαν again means 'the poor', not 'poverty'.

problems.why: 'Received them' suggests hospitality; the Greek refers to those who received the soldiers (as guests/quartering) or perhaps those who received/took in refugees, but context suggests people compelled to billet or support soldiers.
'Loosening poverty' is awkward and unclear; the Greek means 'releasing/relieving their want/need.' The monk solves poverty for the poor, not just 'loosens' it.

problems.quote: he comes bringing some grace alike to rich and poor, to these and to those equally
problems.source_quote: πλουσίων καὶ πενήτων χάριν τινὰ κομίζων ἦλθε καὶ τούτοις κἀκείνοις ὁμοίως
problems.why: Source says 'some grace from rich and poor' (genitive), not 'to'; the monk receives favor, not brings it.
problems.fix: he came bringing some grace from rich and poor alike, to these and to those equally
problems.ruling: πλουσίων καὶ πενήτων is genitive, 'from rich and poor'; monk receives, not brings, grace.

problems.quote: they revel all the time, common enemies of the land, exacting from the farmers what the earth has not produced.
problems.source_quote: ἀλλὰ κωμάζουσι πάντα τὸν χρόνον, κοινοί τινες πολέμιοι τῆς χώρας, ἅπερ οὐκ ἐξήνεγκεν ἡ γῆ, ταῦτα τοὺς γεωργοὺς εἰσπραττόμενοι.
problems.why: 'Revel' (κωμάζουσι) here means 'raise a lament/bewail' in context of lamentation, not festive reveling.
problems.fix: they raise lament all the time, common enemies of the land, exacting from the farmers what the earth has not produced.
problems.ruling: Context of οἰμωγῆς and lamentation demands 'raise a din/clamor,' not festive 'revel.'

problems.quote: he passes by the king as if he were a lifeless thing
problems.source_quote: τὸν βασιλέα μὲν ὥσπερ τὰ ἄψυχα παρέρχεται
problems.why: The subject is the person storm-tossed by misfortunes; 'he passes by the king' suggests the sufferer passes by, but the Greek says the king passes by the sufferer like lifeless things (i.e., ignores him). The agency is reversed.
problems.fix: the king passes him by like a lifeless thing
problems.ruling: τὸν βασιλέα...παρέρχεται: king is accusative object of παρέρχεται, so sufferer passes by king. English 'he passes by the king' is correct, not reversed.

fixed: τοὺς ὑποδεξαμένους refers to those who received the soldiers as guests/quartering; 'those who quartered them' is correct.
λύων τὴν ἔνδειαν means relieving want; 'relieving the latter's want' is correct.
πλουσίων καὶ πενήτων χάριν τινὰ κομίζων ἦλθε: the genitives are source, so 'from rich and poor' is correct.
κωμάζουσι in this context means lamentation, not revelry; 'raise lament' is correct.
τὸν βασιλέα μὲν ὥσπερ τὰ ἄψυχα παρέρχεται: the king is the subject who passes by the sufferer; 'the king passes him by like a lifeless thing' is correct.

problems.quote: to besiege cities from their seat
problems.source_quote: τὰς πόλεις ἐν τῇ καθέδρᾳ πολιορκεῖν
problems.why: 'Seat' suggests the king's own seat/throne; Greek means soldiers besiege cities while sitting/stationed in them (occupation).

problems.quote: The one grants gold, the other the grace of the Spirit
problems.source_quote: ὁ μὲν χρυσὸν, ὁ δὲ πνεύματος χάριν
problems.why: Missing explicit subject identification: 'the one [the king] grants gold, the other [the monk] the grace of the Spirit'—English loses which grants which.
problems.fix: The king grants gold, the monk the grace of the Spirit

problems.quote: For that man is fed with so much food as would not demand deep sleep from a monk
problems.source_quote: Καὶ ἐκεῖνος μὲν γὰρ τοσούτοις τρέφεται σιτίοις, ὅσα οὐκ ἂν ἀπαιτήσειε τὸν μοναχὸν ὕπνον βαθύν
problems.why: Subject confusion: 'that man' refers to the king, but English makes it sound like the monk is fed; 'demand deep sleep from a monk' reverses who sleeps.
problems.fix: For the king is fed with so much food as would not even demand deep sleep of him, yet luxury and drink lull him to sleep, keeping him in bed until day itself.
problems.ruling: ἐκεῖνος = the king; ὅσα οὐκ ἂν ἀπαιτήσειε = food so little it wouldn't induce deep sleep; English reverses both subject and logic

problems.quote: he came bringing some grace from rich and poor alike
problems.source_quote: καὶ πλουσίων καὶ πενήτων χάριν τινὰ κομίζων ἦλθε
problems.why: Grace is brought TO rich and poor, not FROM them; 'from' reverses direction of benefit.
problems.fix: he came bringing some grace to rich and poor alike
problems.ruling: πλουσίων καὶ πενήτων χάριν κομίζων = bringing grace TO rich and poor; 'from' reverses direction of benefit

problems.quote: they raise lament all the time
problems.why: κωμάζω means revel/carouse (ironically: tax-collectors party while oppressing), not 'raise lament'.
problems.ruling: κωμάζω = revel/celebrate, not lament; ironic contrast with preceding οἰμωγῆς; 'raise lament' is wrong meaning

problems.quote: the king passes him by like a lifeless thing
problems.source_quote: τὸν βασιλέα μὲν ὥσπερ τὰ ἄψυχα παρέρχεται
problems.why: Subject/object confusion: the afflicted person passes by the king (as inanimate objects pass by), not king passing by him.
problems.fix: the king is passed by like the inanimate
problems.ruling: τὸν βασιλέα...παρέρχεται = the sufferer passes by the king as one passes lifeless things; English reverses subject/object

problems.quote: like one fleeing a wolf and taking refuge with a hunter
problems.source_quote: ὥσπερ ὁ λύκον ὑποφεύγων, καταφεύγων δὲ ἐπ' ἄνδρα θηρευτὴν
problems.why: ὑποφεύγων means fleeing FROM under/away (wolf flees from hunter), not person fleeing wolf; simile structure inverted.
problems.fix: like a wolf fleeing and taking refuge with a hunter
problems.ruling: ὁ λύκον ὑποφεύγων = the wolf fleeing (from hunter); English makes person flee wolf, inverting the simile

fixed: Subject confusion in first sentence: source has the king as subject of τρέφεται, and the monk as the one who would not demand deep sleep; edited to clarify.
ἐν τῇ καθέδρᾳ πολιορκεῖν means besieging while stationed/occupying, not 'from their seat'; edited.

fixed.quote: For the king is fed with so much food as would not demand deep sleep of a monk
fixed.fix: For the monk is fed only with so much food as would not demand deep sleep, unlike the king
fixed.note: ἐκεῖνος μέν is the monk, set against τὸν δέ (the king lulled by luxury); the English wrongly makes the king the frugal eater, and the proposed fix leaves 'him' in the next clause pointing at the monk.

fixed.quote: he came bringing some grace to rich and poor alike
fixed.fix: he comes bringing some grace to rich and poor alike
fixed.note: 'As soon as he appears, he came' mixes present and past tense and is broken English; the general present fits the description of the monk's character.

fixed.quote: like a wolf fleeing and taking refuge with a hunter
fixed.fix: like one fleeing from a wolf and taking refuge with a hunter
fixed.note: λύκον is the accusative object of ὑποφεύγων, so the person flees from the wolf; the wolf is not the one fleeing to the hunter.

dismissed.why: ἐν τῇ καθέδρᾳ means 'while sitting in camp' or 'from his seat,' not 'occupy and besiege.'
dismissed.note: ἐν τῇ καθέδρᾳ refers to the soldiers being stationed in the cities, which 'occupy and besiege' conveys; 'from his camp' would wrongly shift the action to the king.

dismissed.quote: and to exact from those who quartered them
dismissed.why: τοὺς ὑποδεξαμένους means 'those who received/entertained them' (hosts), not 'quartered them' (military sense).
dismissed.note: 'Those who quartered them' is a correct rendering of the hosts who received billeted soldiers.

dismissed.quote: as if truly being ashamed before the wealthy
dismissed.why: The king harms the poor while sparing the rich, as if ashamed to touch the wealthy; 'being ashamed before' is awkward and slightly off.
dismissed.note: αἰσχύνομαι with an accusative means to feel shame or awe before someone, so 'ashamed before the wealthy' is fair.

dismissed.quote: the king is passed by like the inanimate
dismissed.why: Subject is the sufferer 'he passes by the king,' not 'the king is passed by'; middle voice παρέρχεται with accusative means 'passes by/neglects.'
dismissed.note: The passive voice keeps the meaning (the sufferer passes the king by as though he were lifeless) and the next clause names who acts.
